# Introduction

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known locations in a
tissue. When two tissues are compared, for example a diseased section and a
healthy control, the usual differential expression analysis compares the mean
expression of each gene and ignores where the gene is expressed. A gene can
then look unchanged although its spatial pattern changed, or look changed
although its pattern is the same and only its level differs.

STcompare compares two structurally matched tissues location by location.
For every gene it answers two questions:

| Question | Test | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Is the gene's spatial **pattern** the same in both samples? | Spatial correlation: Pearson's correlation of the two samples over matched pixels, with a permutation p-value that accounts for spatial autocorrelation | `correlationCoef`, `pValuePermute`, `pValuePermuteAdj` |
| Is the gene's expression **level** the same at matched locations? | Spatial similarity: the share of matched pixels where the two values are within a fold change of each other | `percentSimilarity` (descriptive, no p-value) |

The two tests are complementary: a gene can have the same pattern at a
different level (high correlation, low similarity), or the same level with a
different pattern.

This tutorial uses small simulated data that ships with the package and runs in
under a minute. The method is described in Clifton et al. (2026),
[doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btag644](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag644).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(STcompare)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

# Simulated kidneys

`speKidney` is a list of three simulated single-cell datasets, `A`, `B` and
`C`, each a `SpatialExperiment` with one gene called `Gene`, its counts in the
assay `counts`, and the x-y coordinates of the cells in `spatialCoords()`.

```{r data}
data(speKidney)
speKidney$A
```

```{r cells, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Maps of the cells of the simulated kidneys A, B and C, coloured by the expression of Gene: A and C share a pattern and B has the opposite pattern."}
cells <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("A", "B", "C"), function(s) {
  data.frame(spatialCoords(speKidney[[s]]),
             expression = assay(speKidney[[s]], "counts")["Gene", ],
             sample = s)
}))
ggplot(cells, aes(x, y, colour = expression)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~sample) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  theme_void()
```

A and B have the same expression levels but opposite patterns, and A and C have
the same pattern at different levels. Comparing the distributions of the
expression values, which is what a mean-based comparison does, misses both
differences:

```{r boxplot, fig.width = 4, fig.height = 3, out.width = "60%", fig.alt = "Box plots of the expression of Gene in A, B and C: A and B have the same distribution, and C is higher."}
ggplot(cells, aes(sample, expression)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Expression") +
  theme_classic()
```

A and B are indistinguishable by their means, and A and C differ only by a
fold change. STcompare's two tests separate these cases.

# Prepare the input

STcompare compares the same locations in two samples, so the samples must
first be put on a common grid:

1. **Align** the tissues, so that the same coordinates point to the same
   structure in both samples. [STalign](https://jef.works/STalign/) does this
   for sections that are not already aligned; the simulated kidneys are.
2. **Rasterize** both samples **together**, in one call of
   `SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression()`. This aggregates cells or spots into
   pixels of a shared grid, so that a pixel name means the same location in
   every sample. Samples rasterized in separate calls generally do not share
   their grid, and `compareSpatial()` refuses pixels whose coordinates differ.

```{r rasterize}
rast <- SEraster::rasterizeGeneExpression(speKidney, assay_name = "counts",
                                          resolution = 0.2, fun = "mean",
                                          square = FALSE)
rast$A
```

The result is a list of `SpatialExperiment` objects, one per sample, whose
columns are hexagonal pixels and whose assay `pixelval` holds the mean
expression of the cells in each pixel. Pixels are shared where both samples
have cells.

```{r rasterplot, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "The three kidneys rasterized onto one grid of hexagonal pixels, coloured by the mean expression of Gene."}
SEraster::plotRaster(rast$A, plotTitle = "A") +
  SEraster::plotRaster(rast$B, plotTitle = "B") +
  SEraster::plotRaster(rast$C, plotTitle = "C")
```

# Compare two samples

`compareSpatial()` runs both tests for every gene in both samples. It takes
two `SpatialExperiment` objects, or a named list of two, whose names label the
samples in the output. Here we compare A with B.

```{r ab}
ab <- compareSpatial(rast[c("A", "B")], nThreads = 2)
ab
```

The printed header summarises the settings and the counts; the table has one
row per gene. `nThreads` sets the number of threads; the results do not
depend on it, and `options(STcompare.nThreads = 8)` sets it for a whole
session. In an interactive session, `compareSpatial()` also shows a progress
line with an estimate of the remaining time while the permutations run.

A and B are strongly negatively correlated (`correlationCoef` =
`r round(ab$correlationCoef, 3)`): none of the `r ab$nPermutations` null
correlations was as extreme, so the permutation p-value `pValuePermute` is the
smallest possible value, 1/`r sprintf("%d", ab$nPermutations + 1L)`.
`r round(100 * ab$percentSimilarity)`% of their matched pixels are within
two-fold of each other (`percentSimilarity`). Now A and C:

```{r ac}
ac <- compareSpatial(rast[c("A", "C")], nThreads = 2)
as.data.frame(ac)[, c("gene", "correlationCoef", "pValuePermute",
                      "pValuePermuteAdj", "nPermutations", "percentSimilarity",
                      "percentDissimilarityX", "percentDissimilarityY")]
```

A and C are positively correlated (`correlationCoef` =
`r round(ac$correlationCoef, 3)`), yet none of their pixels are within
two-fold: in `r round(100 * ac$percentDissimilarityY)`% of the pixels kept for
the similarity, C is more than twice as high as A.

## Reading the result

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gene`, `nPixels` | The gene and the number of shared pixels. |
| `correlationCoef` | Pearson's correlation of the gene's values in the two samples over the shared pixels. |
| `pValueNaive` | The p-value of `cor.test()`, which assumes that pixels are independent. Neighbouring pixels are not independent, so this value is far too small; it is shown for reference only (see below). |
| `pValuePermuteX`, `pValuePermuteY` | The permutation p-value of each direction: surrogates of the first sample (X) correlated with the second, and surrogates of the second (Y) correlated with the first; each is (b + 1) / (L + 1) for b null correlations at least as extreme as the observed one among the gene's L permutations. Not adjusted, and descriptive: when a gene stops early, the direction that did not reach `exceedances` has an inflated value. |
| `pValuePermute` | The permutation p-value of the gene: the larger of the two directions' sequential p-values (`exceedances` / L for the direction that stopped the gene, (b + 1) / (L + 1) at the limit), which is valid whatever the dependence between the two directions. It equals the larger of `pValuePermuteX` and `pValuePermuteY` for a gene that reached `nPermutations`, and is slightly smaller for a gene that stopped early. It accounts for the spatial autocorrelation of both samples: the null correlations come from surrogates of one sample that keep its spatial autocorrelation but are unrelated to the other sample. Not adjusted; its smallest possible value is 1 / (`nPermutations` + 1). |
| `pValuePermuteAdj` | `pValuePermute` adjusted for multiple testing across the genes of the call (Benjamini-Hochberg by default, `adjustMethod`). Use this column to call a gene significant. |
| `nPermutations`, `stop` | How many permutations the gene used, and why it stopped: `"exceedances"` when it stopped early because its p-value is clearly not small, `"limit"` when it reached the `nPermutations` argument. |
| `deltaStarMedianX`, `deltaStarMedianY` | The median smoothing bandwidth (delta star) chosen for the surrogates of each sample. |
| `deltaGridEdge` | `TRUE` when most surrogates chose the smallest or the largest bandwidth of the grid, a hint to extend the `delta` argument. |
| `percentSimilarity` | The share (a proportion between 0 and 1, despite the name) of the kept pixels whose values are within a fold change of each other, \|log2(y / x)\| <= `foldChange` (1, two-fold, by default). |
| `percentDissimilarityX`, `percentDissimilarityY` | The shares of kept pixels more than `foldChange` higher in the first sample (X) and in the second (Y), also proportions. The three shares add up to 1. The similarity compares fold changes, so it needs values that are not negative: it is `NA` for genes with negative values. |
| `numPixelInThresh`, `t1`, `t2` | The number of pixels kept for the similarity: those above the gene's expression threshold in either sample, `t1` in the first and `t2` in the second (its 5% quantile by default, `minQuantile`). |
| `status`, `message` | `"ok"`; `"skipped"`, with the reason, for a gene that is not tested for correlation because it is constant in a sample (or, with `surrogate = "gaussian"`, detected in few pixels of a sample; see `minDetected` in `?compareSpatial`); or `"failed"`, with the reason, for a gene that could not be tested (for example because of missing values). |

The columns have the names of the legacy functions
`spatialCorrelationGeneExp()` and `spatialSimilarity()` where both report the
same quantity, and a p-value column carries the suffix `Adj` exactly when it is
adjusted across genes: `compareSpatial()` adjusts its combined p-value
(`pValuePermuteAdj`), and the legacy function adjusts each direction on its own
(`pValuePermuteXAdj`, `pValuePermuteYAdj`; see
[Migrating from the legacy functions](#migrating-from-the-legacy-functions)).
`?compareSpatial` documents every column.

`as.data.frame()` turns the result into a plain data frame, and `summary()`
gives the counts:

```{r summary}
summary(ac)
```

## Adaptive permutations: genes that are clearly not significant stop early

The permutation p-value is computed from up to `nPermutations` (10,000 by
default) surrogate pairs, but a gene stops as soon as `exceedances` (10 by
default) null correlations are at least as extreme as the observed one. A
gene whose patterns are unrelated stops after a few dozen permutations,
while a significant gene runs to the limit, which sets the smallest possible
p-value, `1 / (nPermutations + 1)`. For example, two independently simulated
patterns from `simRanPatternRasts`:

```{r early}
data(simRanPatternRasts)
indep <- compareSpatial(simRanPatternRasts[[1]], simRanPatternRasts[[2]],
                        nThreads = 2)
as.data.frame(indep)[, c("correlationCoef", "pValuePermute", "nPermutations",
                         "stop")]
```

This gene stopped after `r indep$nPermutations` permutations, with
`pValuePermute` = `r signif(indep$pValuePermute, 2)`, while A and B used all
`r ab$nPermutations`. The article [How STcompare works](how-STcompare-works.html)
explains why the p-value stays valid when genes stop at different times.

# Visualizing results

`plotGene()` draws one standard figure for a gene of a result: the gene at
native resolution in both samples, on the shared pixels, the similarity class
of every pixel, and the expression at matched pixels with the gene's
statistics. It takes the result, the gene and the two rasterized objects that
`compareSpatial()` compared, in the same order; `native` gives the objects
before rasterization, in the same order, for the native-resolution maps.

```{r plot-ab, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "The standard figure of Gene for A and B: the cells of A and B coloured by expression, the shared pixels coloured by expression, the pixels coloured by similarity class, and a scatter plot of the values at matched pixels with the statistics."}
plotGene(ab, "Gene", rast$A, rast$B, native = speKidney[c("A", "B")])
```

The panels, lettered for a figure legend, one letter for each pair of maps:

- **A**: the cells of A and B coloured by the counts of the gene (the first
  assay of the `native` objects; `nativeAssay` chooses another).
- **B**: the shared pixels coloured by the values that the tests compared,
  here the mean counts `pixelval`. The two maps of a pair share one colour
  scale, so that the colours of the two samples are comparable
  (`sharedScale = FALSE` gives each map its own). Pixels that one sample
  lacks, which the tests did not use, are light grey in every map.
- **C**: the similarity class of every pixel: within two-fold in both samples
  (blue), more than two-fold higher in A (orange) or in B (pink), or below
  the expression threshold in both (grey). The legend gives the share of each
  class among the pixels above the threshold, so the share of similar pixels
  is `percentSimilarity`.
- **D**: the values at matched pixels, A horizontally and B vertically, in the
  same colours; the solid line is y = x, the dashed lines bound the two-fold
  band and the dotted lines are the thresholds `t1` and `t2` (the figure's
  caption is the key). The subtitle gives the gene's row of the result:
  `correlationCoef` (r), `pValuePermute` (p, marked "minimum" when it is the
  smallest value the permutations can give), `pValuePermuteAdj`,
  `pValueNaive`, the number of permutations and `percentSimilarity`.

The anti-correlation of A and B is the falling band of points in D, and C
shows where the levels differ: around the edge of the kidney A is higher
(orange), in its centre B is higher (pink). For A and C, the pattern is the
same, so the points in D line up with a positive slope, but C is more than
two-fold higher at every pixel, so every point lies above the band and every
pixel is pink:

```{r plot-ac, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "The standard figure of Gene for A and C: the same pattern in both, every pixel more than two-fold higher in C."}
plotGene(ac, "Gene", rast$A, rast$C, native = speKidney[c("A", "C")])
```

Without `native`, the figure has one row: the pixel maps (A), the similarity
classes (B) and the matched pixels (C). `panels` selects panels, `transform = "log1p"` draws the maps and the scatter
axes on a log scale (useful for counts that span orders of magnitude), and
`?plotGene` describes every option. For a result with many genes,
`plotOverview(result)` draws the overview of all of them: the correlation of
every gene against its adjusted p-value, the distribution of the similarity,
and the two against each other, with the significant genes coloured. The
[case studies](https://jef.works/STcompare/articles/acute-kidney-injury-10x-visium-rasterized.html)
show it.

## Saving and customizing a figure

The figure is a [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) of ggplot2
panels, so `ggplot2::ggsave()` writes it in any format, with the size in
inches. With the default text size (`baseSize = 10` points), a height of 6.5
suits the two-row figure with the native maps and 3.5 the one row without
them. The maps keep the shape of the tissue, so the tissue sets the width the
figure needs, and a wider canvas only adds blank space at the sides: these
kidneys, taller than wide, fill 7 by 6.5 and 8.5 by 3.5, while a square tissue
needs about 10 by 6.5 and 11 by 3.5.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
fig <- plotGene(ab, "Gene", rast$A, rast$B, native = speKidney[c("A", "B")])
ggsave("Gene-A-vs-B.pdf", fig, width = 7, height = 6.5)
ggsave("Gene-A-vs-B.png", fig, width = 7, height = 6.5, dpi = 300)
```

Every text, legend key and point of the figure is scaled from `baseSize`, so
a journal figure needs only a smaller base size: `baseSize = 7` for the full
width of a page (180 mm; these kidneys fill 125 mm of it at a height of
115 mm), and `baseSize = 6` with `ncol = 2` for a single column (90 mm).

```{r save-journal, eval = FALSE}
fig <- plotGene(ab, "Gene", rast$A, rast$B, native = speKidney[c("A", "B")],
                baseSize = 7)
ggsave("Gene-A-vs-B-125mm.pdf", fig, width = 125, height = 115, units = "mm")
```

Patchwork's `&` operator applies a ggplot2 theme to every panel, and `+`
changes the figure's annotation; for example, to draw only the similarity
panels in a larger serif font, without the panel letters:

```{r customize, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "The similarity map and the scatter plot of Gene for A and B, in a serif font and without panel letters."}
plotGene(ab, "Gene", rast$A, rast$B, panels = c("similarity", "scatter")) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = NULL) &
  theme(text = element_text(family = "serif", size = 12))
```

# Why permutation p-values? A calibration check

Neighbouring pixels have similar values: the patterns are spatially
autocorrelated. Two unrelated but smooth patterns can therefore have a sizeable
correlation by chance, much more often than `cor.test()` expects from
independent observations. `simRanPatternRasts` holds 100 independently
simulated, spatially autocorrelated patterns rasterized onto one grid, so any
two of them are unrelated. We compare 50 disjoint pairs, (1, 2), (3, 4), and
so on, with a different seed for each pair, and collect the results.

```{r calibration}
pairs <- matrix(seq_along(simRanPatternRasts), nrow = 2)
calibration <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(k) {
  res <- compareSpatial(simRanPatternRasts[[pairs[1, k]]],
                        simRanPatternRasts[[pairs[2, k]]],
                        tests = "correlation", nPermutations = 1000,
                        seed = k, nThreads = 2, verbose = FALSE)
  as.data.frame(res)
}))
nrow(calibration)
summary(calibration$nPermutations)
```

Most pairs stopped after a few dozen permutations, so the 50 tests take a few
seconds. The null hypothesis is true for every pair, so a calibrated test
gives p < 0.05 for about 5% of them:

```{r calibration-counts}
c(naive = sum(calibration$pValueNaive < 0.05),
  permutation = sum(calibration$pValuePermute < 0.05))
c(naive = sum(p.adjust(calibration$pValueNaive, "BH") < 0.05),
  permutation = sum(p.adjust(calibration$pValuePermute, "BH") < 0.05))
```

`r sum(calibration$pValueNaive < 0.05)` of 50 naive p-values are below 0.05, and
`r sum(p.adjust(calibration$pValueNaive, "BH") < 0.05)` pairs remain "significant"
after the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The permutation test gives
`r sum(calibration$pValuePermute < 0.05)` of 50, in line with the 2.5 expected by chance:
the one-sided binomial p-value of seeing at least that many is
`r format.pval(binom.test(sum(calibration$pValuePermute < 0.05), 50, 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value, digits = 2)`,
against
`r format.pval(binom.test(sum(calibration$pValueNaive < 0.05), 50, 0.05, alternative = "greater")$p.value, digits = 2)`
for the naive test. After the adjustment, the permutation test gives
`r sum(p.adjust(calibration$pValuePermute, "BH") < 0.05)`.

```{r calibration-plot, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Histograms of the p-values of 50 unrelated pairs: the naive p-values pile up near 0, the permutation p-values do not."}
pvalues <- rbind(
  data.frame(test = "naive (cor.test)", p = calibration$pValueNaive),
  data.frame(test = "permutation (compareSpatial)",
             p = calibration$pValuePermute))
ggplot(pvalues, aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50 * 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~test) +
  labs(x = "p-value of 50 unrelated pairs", y = "Pairs") +
  theme_classic()
```

Under the null hypothesis, p-values are uniformly distributed (dashed line).
The naive p-values pile up near 0; the permutation p-values do not. Many
permutation p-values are close to 1: a pair whose patterns are clearly
unrelated reaches 10 exceedances within its first few permutations and stops
with p = 10 / L, for example 1 after 10 permutations.

# Migrating from the legacy functions

The functions of earlier versions are still available, unchanged in their
interface. They are computed by the same compiled engine and reproduce the
published analyses exactly. `compareSpatial()` is the recommended entry point
for new analyses.

| Earlier function | `compareSpatial()` |
|---|---|
| `spatialCorrelationGeneExp(list(A = a, B = b))` | `compareSpatial(list(A = a, B = b), tests = "correlation")` |
| `spatialCorrelationGeneExpIterPermutations()` (100, then 1000 permutations for promising genes) | adaptive permutations, the default (`exceedances = 10`, `nPermutations = 10000`) |
| `spatialSimilarity(list(a, b))` | `compareSpatial(a, b, tests = "similarity")` |
| `correlationCoef`, `pValueNaive` | the same |
| `pValuePermuteX`, `pValuePermuteY`: the raw p-value of each direction; `pValuePermuteXAdj`, `pValuePermuteYAdj`: each adjusted across genes; significant when both adjusted values are below 0.05 (before version 2.0.0 there were no `Adj` columns: `spatialCorrelationGeneExpIterPermutations()` returned the adjusted values as `pValuePermuteX` and `pValuePermuteY`, and `spatialCorrelationGeneExp()`, which adjusted one gene at a time, returned unadjusted values under these names) | `pValuePermuteX`, `pValuePermuteY`: the raw p-value of each direction; `pValuePermute` = the gene's p-value, the larger of the two directions' sequential p-values; `pValuePermuteAdj` = `pValuePermute` adjusted across genes; significant when `pValuePermuteAdj` < 0.05 |
| `deltaStarMedianX`, `deltaStarMedianY` | the same |
| `percentSimilarity`, `percentDissimilarityX`, `percentDissimilarityY` | the same |
| `numPixelInThresh`, `t1`, `t2` | the same |

The differences in the results:

- `correlationCoef`, `pValueNaive` and the similarity scores are identical.
- The permutation p-values differ: `compareSpatial()` draws independent
  permutations for each gene and direction (the earlier functions share one
  set across genes), stops early for genes that are clearly not significant,
  gives its surrogates the gene's own values (`surrogate = "remap"`; the
  earlier functions' surrogates have nearly normal values,
  `surrogate = "gaussian"`), and adjusts one combined p-value per gene. On the
  published kidney analysis the two approaches agree on the significance of
  98% of the genes; on the brain analysis `compareSpatial()` finds 45 more
  genes among 325, which the remapped surrogates have the power to detect (see
  [Parameters, performance and reproducibility](parameters-performance-reproducibility.html)).
- `compareSpatial()` tests every gene that is not constant in a sample,
  including genes detected in a few pixels, for which the remapped surrogates
  give calibrated p-values. With `surrogate = "gaussian"` such genes are
  skipped (`minDetected`), because gaussian surrogates give them p-values that
  are far too small.
- `compareSpatial()` checks that the shared pixels have the same coordinates,
  uses the genes present in both samples, and reports genes that are skipped or
  cannot be tested in its `status` and `message` columns instead of stopping.

The plotting functions of earlier versions are also unchanged:
`plotCorrelationGeneExp()` draws the scatter plot of a gene from the
rasterized objects and a correlation result, and `linearRegression()` and
`pixelClass()` draw the scatter plot and the map of the similarity classes
from a `spatialSimilarity()` result, which `savePlots()` writes to files.
`plotGene()` draws all of this, and more, from one `compareSpatial()` result.

```{r legacy-plots, fig.height = 6, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.alt = "The legacy plots of Gene for A and B: the scatter plot of plotCorrelationGeneExp() above, and the scatter plot and the map of the similarity classes of linearRegression() and pixelClass() below."}
simAB <- spatialSimilarity(rast[c("A", "B")])
plotCorrelationGeneExp(rast[c("A", "B")], ab, "Gene") /
  (linearRegression(simAB, "Gene") + pixelClass(simAB, "Gene"))
```

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
